# Job Search Campaign — Aug 2026

> **Private.** This folder is gitignored (`job-search/` in `.gitignore`) — it must never be committed or pushed. The repo has two public GitHub remotes.

**Goal:** Backend / full-stack SDE role at ₹15–30 LPA · 1.5 yrs experience · currently ₹8 LPA at Visionify.ai.

---

## Status

| Asset | State | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Resume (one-page LaTeX, Overleaf) | ✅ Done Aug 17 | Overleaf (paste-in; not in repo) |
| LinkedIn profile | ✅ Done Aug 17 | linkedin.com/in/ayusharyan1309 |
| Naukri kit | ✅ Built Aug 18 | `naukri-profile-kit.html` (this folder) |
| Instahyre kit | ✅ Built Aug 18 | `instahyre-profile-kit.html` (this folder) |
| Wellfound answers | ✅ Written Aug 19 | Below |
| Job-switch narrative | ✅ Drafted Aug 19 | `job-switch-narrative.md` (this folder) — 4 facts to fill in |
| Outreach playbook (referrals, cover letters, recruiter msgs) | ✅ Built Aug 19 | `outreach-templates.md` (this folder) |
| Mobile access to these notes | ✅ Built Aug 19 | Portfolio site → tap "Ayush." 5×. See `README.md` |
| Cutshort, BigShyft, Talent500, Weekday, TopHire | ⬜ Register (reuse Instahyre pitch) | — |
| Naukri/Instahyre profiles actually updated | ⬜ Execute the kit checklists | — |

## Key decisions

- **Expected CTC everywhere: ₹18 LPA.** Recruiters filter by max budget; at 1.5 YOE most 15–20 searches cap near 20. ₹18 stays inside those searches and anchors above 15. Quote higher in HR calls at known 25+ payers — the profile number earns the invite, not the offer.
- **₹8 → ₹18 is a normal early-career jump (2–2.5x).** Product companies pay to band, not percentage hikes. Script for "100%+ hike" pushback: *"My current package is below market because I joined an early-stage startup; I'm benchmarking to the market rate for my skill set, not to my current CTC."* 25–30 LPA means cracking top-tier product-company interviews (DSA + system design bar).
- **Enter current CTC honestly** (mismatch at BGV/offer stage kills offers). Quote fixed vs. variable clearly.
- **Every platform tells the identical story** — same titles, dates, metrics, skill-years as the resume. Companies cross-check.
- **Naukri mechanics:** freshness ranks (touch profile every 2–3 days); notice period is the #2 filter; upload the resume PDF; apply within 24h of postings; watch "Search appearances" weekly.
- **Instahyre/Cutshort mechanics:** employer-outreach driven — the card (pitch + top skills + CTC + notice) does the selling; respond to every invite within a day or two, even declines.

## Wellfound content (written Aug 19)

### Achievements
- Own a production alerting service at Visionify.ai that processes 10K+ workplace-safety events/day with sub-150ms end-to-end latency across Email, Microsoft Teams, and WhatsApp — and keeps delivering through peak bursts.
- Lead an entire product, PalletVision, end to end as an SDE-1 — the computer-vision detection model, backend services, and frontend — now powering productivity, grading, and dimensional analytics for pallet manufacturers.
- Architected backend microservices for a global event-CRM platform that held 100K+ concurrent users during live international events.
- Built a fault-tolerant data-ingestion pipeline handling 2K+ files per batch (50K+ rows each) with schema validation and automatic retries.
- Shipped a production RAG chatbot for my portfolio on a zero-cost serverless stack (Cloudflare Workers AI + Vercel) — it answers recruiters' questions about my work: https://ayush-aryan1309-portfolio.vercel.app
- Delivered a full Flutter marketplace app single-handedly in my first internship and cut backend latency ~30% with caching and endpoint optimization.

### "What are you looking for in your next job?"
A backend or full-stack role where I own services end to end — design, build, ship, and run them in production. I'm at my best in small teams that move fast: at Visionify I lead a product across the CV model, backend, and frontend, and I want more of that scope, not less. I care about distributed systems at real scale — my current work runs on Kafka, Redis, and event-driven pipelines — and I'm drawn to teams shipping GenAI features to production rather than prototyping them. Product-first companies where engineers talk to users are exactly my fit.

### Markets (pick 4–5, in order)
1. Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning
2. SaaS / Enterprise Software (B2B)
3. Fintech (hook: Eventstrat payment workflows)
4. Developer Tools / Infrastructure
5. E-commerce / Marketplaces (optional)

### Spring Boot depth answer (for "describe your experience in depth" fields)
I've used Spring Boot as my primary framework for 1.5+ years, building and running production microservices at two companies.

At Eventstrat.ai, I architected Spring Boot microservices for a global event-CRM platform that supported 100K+ concurrent users during live international events. I worked across the Spring Cloud stack — Spring Cloud Gateway at the edge, Eureka for service discovery, OpenFeign for inter-service calls, and Resilience4j for circuit breaking and retries — so services stayed responsive when a downstream dependency degraded. I built a fault-tolerant bulk data-ingestion pipeline handling 50K+ rows per file and 2K+ files per batch, with schema validation, asynchronous chunked processing, and automatic retries for failed records. I also built exhibitor payment workflows (multi-installment plans, event-specific tax calculation, scheduled payment reminders) and event-driven notifications using spring-kafka producers/consumers with Redis for hot data.

At Visionify.ai, I own an event-driven alerting service built on the same Java/Spring Boot patterns — it processes 10K+ workplace-safety events/day and fans out to Email, Microsoft Teams, and WhatsApp with sub-150ms end-to-end response times and fault-tolerant routing under burst load.

Data layer: Hibernate/JPA against MySQL and MongoDB, with Liquibase for schema migrations. Caching: Redis — in my wellness-platform project, Redis-based slot caching cut scheduling latency ~40% and eliminated double-booking. Real-time delivery: WebSockets and Firebase FCM. Operations: Spring Actuator metrics into Prometheus/Grafana, Dockerized deployments through Jenkins CI/CD.

Day to day I care about clean layered architecture, DTO validation, global exception handling, and idempotent Kafka consumers — services that are boring to operate.

*(Caution: interviewers probe this line by line — trim anything not genuinely hands-on, e.g. Eureka/Resilience4j if only configured once.)*

## Platforms & agencies

**Done:** LinkedIn, Naukri, Instahyre, Wellfound (in progress).
**Register next:** Cutshort, BigShyft, Talent500 (ANSR/GCCs), Weekday, TopHire (selective — apply anyway).
**Agencies (employer-paid, free for candidates):** Careernet, Xpheno do product-company volume; ABC/Randstad/Michael Page skew senior. Naukri already exposes you to agency sourcing.
**Rules:** never pay any fee (scam test) · approve every agency submission · state ₹18+ floor upfront · track every submission (company + channel) to avoid duplicate applications.
**Skip:** foundit, Indeed (low value for product roles), Turing/Crossover (different career path).

## Next targets (priority order, set Aug 19)

1. ~~**Job-switch narrative**~~ ✅ Drafted Aug 19 → `job-switch-narrative.md`. Ayush must fill in: real Eventstrat exit reason, exact stint months, notice period, reference-handling stance. Then rehearse the 30-second version aloud.
2. **Interview prep** — DSA mediums consistently; LLD/machine coding; Java/Spring internals (@Transactional, bean lifecycle, concurrency, JVM memory); Kafka/Redis depth. Rehearse the alerting service and ingestion pipeline as system-design stories.
3. **Target company list (~30)** — reach 25–30 LPA / core 15–22 / backup 12–15 + BMU alumni referral outreach against specific job IDs.
4. **Execute platform checklists** + Naukri freshness touch every 2–3 days.
5. **GitHub polish** — pinned repos; production-grade README for wellness-app-backend (architecture sketch, setup). `GITHUB_PROFILE_README.md` in this repo should be live on the profile.
6. **HR endgame** — salary conversation script, notice-period handling, competing-offer playbook.

## Links

- Portfolio: https://ayush-aryan1309-portfolio.vercel.app
- GitHub: https://github.com/ayusharyan1309
- LinkedIn: https://linkedin.com/in/ayusharyan1309
- Personal email for signups: ayusharyan1309@gmail.com (never the Visionify one)

files.content:
# Job-Switch Narrative — the "why are you moving again?" answer

> **Private.** Gitignored folder — never commit or push.

## The problem you're solving

Your timeline reads: Eventstrat ~7 months → Visionify ~11 months → looking again at ~1.5 years total. An interviewer's silent worry is *"this person will leave us in a year too."* You cannot erase the dates, so the narrative's only job is to make each move look **pulled by a step-up, not pushed by a problem** — and to make the next move look like the one you'll stay in.

The arc you're selling: **exposure → ownership → scale.**
Eventstrat gave you scale exposure (100K+ concurrent users). Visionify gave you ownership (a whole product, end to end, as an SDE-1). The next company is where ownership and scale finally combine — and where the growth path to senior is internal, so there's no reason to move again.

---

## The 30-second answer (memorize this one)

> "I've been deliberate about both moves. I started at Eventstrat, an early-stage startup, building Spring Boot microservices for an event platform that held 100K+ concurrent users — great scale exposure very early. Visionify offered me something I couldn't get by staying: full ownership of a product — I lead PalletVision end to end, the CV model, backend, and frontend, and I also run a production alerting service doing 10K+ events a day. So I've had scale exposure and I've had ownership. What I'm looking for now is the place where they combine — larger systems, senior engineers to learn from, and a growth path to senior within the same company. That's why this move is the one I intend to settle into."

Deliver it in one breath, calm, no apology in the tone. You are describing a plan, not defending a record.

---

## Question-by-question

### "Why only 7 months at Eventstrat?"

> "Eventstrat was an early-stage startup and an incredible learning density — I shipped microservices, a bulk ingestion pipeline, and payment workflows in those months. When Visionify approached me with end-to-end ownership of a product, that was a genuine step up in scope, not a sideways hop. Short, but I left with real production systems shipped, and on good terms."

**⚠️ Personalize:** this is the "pulled by a better offer" version. If the real reason was different — project wound down, funding, contract role, layoff — say *that* instead, plainly and without blame ("the project I was hired for was wound down; I used it as the push to find a bigger role"). Interviewers forgive almost any true reason at 0–1 YOE; they don't forgive a story that wobbles under two follow-up questions.

### "Why leave Visionify after a year? You lead a whole product there."

> "That's exactly why. Visionify gave me ownership very early, and I've delivered on it — PalletVision is in production for pallet manufacturers, and my alerting service processes 10K+ safety events a day at sub-150ms latency. But it's a small team: I'm the backend depth on my product. I've grown to the edge of what the role can teach me. I want to work on larger-scale distributed systems alongside engineers senior to me — I learn fastest with people to be wrong in front of. That's not something Visionify can restructure for me; it's a function of company size."

This answer is strong because it praises Visionify while making the move inevitable. Never let it drift into complaints (workload, salary, management).

### "How do we know you won't leave us in a year too?"

> "Look at why I moved each time — a specific step-up, and each one shows in what I shipped. I'm not optimizing for the fastest offer this time; I'm optimizing for a company where the next two levels of growth are internal. If I can go from SDE-1 to senior here, there's nothing to move for. Frankly, switching jobs is expensive for me too — I'd rather compound in one place."

### "Is this move about money?"

> "Compensation matters, but it's the outcome of the move, not the reason. The reason is scale and the engineers I'll work with. I joined an early-stage startup below market, so yes, I expect this move to correct that to market rate — but I've turned down thinking about roles that were only a salary bump."

(Keeps you honest, pre-empts the ₹8→₹18 question, and hands the recruiter your benchmarking script from CAMPAIGN.md.)

### "Does Visionify know you're looking?" / notice period

Answer factually and briefly — never elaborate. "My notice period is X days; I'll serve it professionally / it's negotiable." Nothing about internal conversations.

---

## Red lines — never say

- Anything negative about Eventstrat or Visionify (chaos, management, pay, hours). Every complaint transfers to *you* in the interviewer's mind.
- "Money" as the leading reason — it can be *a* reason, never the first sentence.
- "No growth at Visionify" phrased as blame. The line is *"I've grown to the edge of what a small team can offer"* — company size, not company failure.
- Dates that differ from your resume/Naukri/LinkedIn by even a month. BGV cross-checks everything.
- "I'll stay 5 years, promise." Unverifiable promises sound weakest. Point at the *mechanism* (internal growth path) instead.

## Delivery notes

- Rehearse the 30-second version aloud until it's boring to you. It should sound like the tenth time you've said it, because it will be.
- Every answer ends facing **forward** (what you want next), never backward (what was wrong before).
- If the interviewer keeps drilling, don't grow the story — repeat the same facts calmly. Consistency under pressure *is* the answer.
- Bridge out of this topic into strength: "...and that scale interest is why I'd love to talk about how you run X here."

---

## ⚠️ Fill in before first interview (only you know these)

1. **Real reason for leaving Eventstrat** — pulled by Visionify's offer, or pushed (project/funding/contract end)? Pick the true one; adjust the script above.
2. **Exact months** for both stints — must match resume, LinkedIn, Naukri, and what HR will see in BGV (offer/relieving letters).
3. **Your notice period at Visionify** — the exact number of days, and whether it's buyable/negotiable.
4. **Anything sensitive** — e.g., if Visionify leadership must not find out you're looking, decide now what you'll say when a recruiter asks for a current-manager reference (standard answer: "references after offer stage, please").

# Outreach Playbook — referrals, cover letters, recruiter messages

> **Private.** Gitignored folder — never commit or push.
> Fill `{...}` placeholders before sending. Always use ayusharyan1309@gmail.com, never the Visionify email.

## Your paste-anywhere quick-facts block

Use this as the base of every message — trim per context, never contradict it:

> SDE-1 (backend/full-stack), 1.5+ yrs — Java, Spring Boot, Kafka, Redis, AWS, Docker.
> At Visionify.ai I lead PalletVision end to end (CV model + backend + frontend) and own an alerting service doing 10K+ events/day at sub-150ms. Previously built microservices at Eventstrat.ai for an event platform holding 100K+ concurrent users.
> Portfolio: https://ayush-aryan1309-portfolio.vercel.app · GitHub: https://github.com/ayusharyan1309 · LinkedIn: https://linkedin.com/in/ayusharyan1309

---

## 1. Asking for referrals

### The rules (these matter more than the wording)

1. **Always ask against a specific job ID/link.** "Any openings?" gets ignored; "Can you refer me for req #4521?" gets a yes/no.
2. **Make it one-click easy.** Attach the resume PDF and the job link in the *first* message — never make them ask.
3. **Short.** 5–6 lines max on LinkedIn. Nobody reads referral essays.
4. **Give them an out.** "No pressure if it's not convenient" doubles response rates — people refer more willingly when they don't feel cornered.
5. **They get paid.** Most companies pay employees a referral bonus — you're offering them money, not begging a favor. Write with that posture.
6. **Log every ask** (company, person, date, job ID) so you never double-ask or double-apply. Duplicate applications can void a referral.

### Template A — BMU alumni (your warmest channel)

> Hi {Name}, I'm Ayush — also from BML Munjal (CSE, {their batch relation, e.g. "a couple of years junior"}). I saw you're at {Company} and they have an opening for {role title} ({job link}). I'm an SDE-1 with 1.5 yrs in Java/Spring Boot/Kafka — currently leading a product end to end at Visionify.ai. Would you be open to referring me? Resume attached, and happy to share anything else you need. No pressure at all if it's not convenient — either way, great to connect with BMU folks in the industry.

### Template B — cold employee (no shared background)

> Hi {Name}, I came across your profile while researching {Company}'s {team} team. I'm applying for {role title} ({job link}) — backend SDE with 1.5 yrs on Java/Spring/Kafka, currently owning a production alerting service (10K+ events/day, sub-150ms) at Visionify.ai. If my profile looks like a fit to you, would you consider referring me? Resume attached so it's zero effort on your end. Totally understand if not — thanks either way!

### Template C — former colleague / someone who knows your work

> Hey {Name}! Hope {Company} is treating you well. I'm finally making my move — targeting backend roles, and {Company} has one that fits perfectly: {job link}. You've seen my work up close — would you refer me? Resume attached. Also happy to hop on a call if you want a refresher on what I've been building since.

### Follow-up (one only, after 5–7 days of silence)

> Hi {Name}, just floating this back up in case it got buried — the {role title} opening at {Company}. If it's not something you can help with, absolutely no worries; a "can't right now" is a totally fine answer. Thanks!

**Never send a second follow-up.** Move to the next person at the same company (2–3 asks per company is fine, spaced out; don't blast 10 employees the same day — referral systems flag it).

### After they refer you

> Thank you so much, {Name} — really appreciate it. I'll keep you posted on how it goes. If there's ever anything I can help you with, say the word.

Then actually update them at each stage (interview, offer, rejection). People who hear back refer you again elsewhere — this is how a network compounds.

---

## 2. Cover letters

### When to bother

In India, 90% of applications don't read cover letters — **skip them for Naukri/Instahyre/referral routes.** Write one only when: (a) the form has a required field, (b) it's a Wellfound/startup application where the founder reads it, or (c) you're cold-emailing a hiring manager (the email *is* the cover letter).

### Structure — 4 moves, ~150 words, never a full page

1. **Hook (1 line):** name the role + the one thing that makes you relevant. No "I am writing to apply for…"
2. **Proof (2–3 lines):** two achievements with numbers, chosen to mirror *their* JD keywords.
3. **Fit (1–2 lines):** one specific thing about *their* product/stack and why it pulls you. This line is the whole reason the letter exists — it proves you're not mass-applying.
4. **Ask (1 line):** direct and confident.

### Master template

> Hi {Name / "team"},
>
> I'm applying for {role} — I'm a backend SDE (1.5+ yrs, Java/Spring Boot/Kafka) who currently leads a product end to end at Visionify.ai.
>
> Two things from my work that map to this role: I own a production alerting service processing 10K+ events/day at sub-150ms across Email/Teams/WhatsApp, and at Eventstrat.ai I built Spring Boot microservices for an event platform that held 100K+ concurrent users, including a fault-tolerant ingestion pipeline (2K+ files/batch, 50K+ rows each).
>
> {FIT LINE — write fresh every time. e.g.: "I've followed how {Company} handles {their scale/problem} — that's exactly the kind of system I want to build at larger scale."}
>
> I'd love to talk. Resume attached; my portfolio (with a production RAG chatbot I shipped) is at https://ayush-aryan1309-portfolio.vercel.app.
>
> — Ayush Aryan · ayusharyan1309@gmail.com

### Customization checklist (per application, 5 minutes)

- [ ] Swap the two proof points to match the JD's top keywords (Kafka-heavy JD → lead with alerting; scale-heavy → lead with 100K concurrent).
- [ ] Write the fit line from their actual product/engineering blog/JD — never reuse it.
- [ ] Addressed to a name if findable (LinkedIn: "{Company} engineering manager").
- [ ] Under 160 words. If it scrolls, cut proof, never the fit line.

---

## 3. Recruiter messages

### Cold DM to a recruiter/hiring manager on LinkedIn

> Hi {Name}, I saw {Company} is hiring for {role} ({link/req ID}). Quick pitch: backend SDE, 1.5+ yrs, Java/Spring Boot/Kafka/Redis — currently leading a product end to end at Visionify.ai, previously built for 100K+ concurrent users at Eventstrat. Expected CTC ₹18 LPA, notice {X days}. Resume attached — worth a conversation?

(Recruiters *want* CTC + notice upfront — it saves them a screening call. This is the one message where leading with those numbers helps you.)

### Replying to inbound recruiter outreach — interested

> Hi {Name}, thanks for reaching out — this looks like a genuine fit. Quick facts so you can qualify me fast: 1.5+ yrs backend (Java/Spring Boot/Kafka/Redis/AWS), currently SDE-1 at Visionify.ai leading a product end to end. Current CTC ₹8 LPA (joined an early-stage startup below market), expecting ₹18 LPA — benchmarked to market for my skill set. Notice: {X days}. Happy to talk this week — what times work?

### Replying — not interested (always reply; recruiters recycle candidates)

> Hi {Name}, thanks for thinking of me. This one isn't the right fit ({reason: role/stack/location}), but I'm actively looking — backend roles, Java/Spring/Kafka, ₹18 LPA+, {cities}. If something closer comes across your desk, I'd love to hear about it.

### When a recruiter asks "why such a high hike?" (the ₹8→₹18 script, from CAMPAIGN.md)

> "My current package is below market because I joined an early-stage startup — I'm benchmarking to the market rate for my skill set, not to my current CTC. Happy for the interviews to validate that."

---

## 4. Cold email to a hiring manager (no job posting)

Subject lines that get opened: `Backend SDE — Kafka/Spring, 10K events/day in prod — {Company}` or `Referred by {name}: backend role on {team}`.

> Hi {Name},
>
> I'm reaching out directly because {Company}'s {team/product} is exactly the kind of system I want to work on — {one specific sentence about their engineering}.
>
> I'm a backend SDE (1.5+ yrs, Java/Spring Boot/Kafka). At Visionify.ai I lead a product end to end and own an alerting service doing 10K+ events/day at sub-150ms; at Eventstrat.ai I built microservices behind 100K+ concurrent users.
>
> If you're hiring — or expect to — I'd love 15 minutes. Resume attached; portfolio at https://ayush-aryan1309-portfolio.vercel.app.
>
> Thanks,
> Ayush Aryan · ayusharyan1309@gmail.com · {phone}

Follow up once after 5–7 days ("floating this up — happy to be pointed to whoever's hiring for backend"). Then stop.

---

## 5. Post-interview thank-you (optional in India, but zero-cost signal)

Send within 24h, only after rounds with hiring managers (not HR screens):

> Hi {Name}, thanks for the conversation today — I especially enjoyed digging into {specific topic discussed}. It sharpened my interest in the role. Looking forward to next steps, and happy to provide anything else you need.

---

## Cadence & hygiene

- **Batch:** 5–10 referral asks or cold messages per day beats 50 in one burst (spam filters, and you can't handle 50 parallel conversations anyway).
- **Track everything** in one sheet: Company · Role/JD link · Channel (referral/direct/recruiter/agency) · Contact · Date · Status. One company = one active channel — duplicates kill referrals and confuse agencies.
- **Attachments:** always the same resume PDF, filename `Ayush_Aryan_SDE_Resume.pdf`. Never a Google Doc link (looks unfinished, permissions break).
- **Timing:** LinkedIn messages land best Tue–Thu, 9–11am. Sunday-night Naukri profile touch = Monday-morning recruiter searches.

files.content:
# Application long-answers

Written Aug 19 for application fields asking for depth. Pair with the Spring
Boot depth answer in `CAMPAIGN.md`.

1. [Most technically complex challenge](#1-most-technically-complex-challenge)
2. [One thing you're good at that not many others are](#2-one-thing-youre-good-at-technically-that-not-many-others-are)

---

# 1. Most technically complex challenge

**Which story to tell:** the Eventstrat bulk ingestion pipeline. It beats the
Visionify alerting service and PalletVision for this specific question because
the engineering problems are classic and layered (memory, partial failure,
idempotency, backpressure, concurrency) — there's a real answer at every
follow-up. Lead with PalletVision instead only if the role is CV/ML-leaning or
the interviewer specifically wants current work.

**⚠️ Verify before you send it** — see the checklist at the bottom. Anything you
can't defend line by line, cut.

---

## The answer

**Context.** At Eventstrat.ai I worked on an event-CRM platform used by
organisers running large international events — the same platform that held
100K+ concurrent users during live event windows. Organisers don't enter data by
hand; they arrive with exports from ticketing partners, sponsor portals and
previous events, and they need all of it live in the CRM *before the doors
open*. In practice that meant bulk uploads of 2,000+ files in a single batch,
each file carrying up to 50,000 rows.

Owning that ingestion path end to end was the hardest thing I've built.

**Why the obvious approach doesn't work.** The naive version is: accept the
upload, parse the file, validate the rows, insert them, return success. That
breaks on every axis at this scale.

- *Memory* — materialising 50,000 parsed rows per file, across concurrent
  uploads, puts the heap under real pressure and eventually OOMs the service.
- *Time* — row-by-row inserts turn a single large file into minutes and a full
  batch into hours. An HTTP request cannot stay open that long, and the client
  times out long before the work finishes.
- *All-or-nothing transactions* — one malformed row at position 49,999 rolls
  back the entire file. Organisers' real-world data is messy: blank emails,
  dates in three formats, duplicate registrations. A pipeline that refuses
  everything because of a handful of bad rows is useless to them.
- *Retry semantics* — if the job dies halfway, the only recovery is re-uploading
  the file, which duplicates everything already written.
- *Blast radius* — ingestion runs while the platform is serving a live event. A
  bulk job that saturates the database degrades the experience for 100K+
  concurrent users, which is far worse than a slow import.

So the real problem wasn't "parse a file." It was: **process very large,
untrusted, partially-invalid data asynchronously, resumably, and without
destabilising a live system.**

**What I built.** A staged asynchronous pipeline in Spring Boot:

1. **Accept fast.** The upload endpoint does almost nothing — it persists the
   raw file, creates a job record with a status, emits a message for downstream
   processing, and returns immediately with a job ID. The HTTP request is fully
   decoupled from the work. The client polls the job instead of holding a
   connection open.

2. **Stream, never slurp.** The processing stage reads the file as a stream
   rather than loading it into memory. Memory use becomes a function of chunk
   size, not file size — which is what makes 50,000-row files behave the same as
   500-row ones.

3. **Validate per row, report per row.** Each row is checked against a schema:
   required fields, type and format coercion (dates and phone numbers were the
   worst offenders), and reference checks against existing entities. Crucially,
   an invalid row does **not** abort the batch. It's recorded with its row
   number and a human-readable reason and the pipeline moves on.

4. **Chunk the work.** Valid rows are grouped into fixed-size chunks, and each
   chunk is its own transaction and its own unit of retry. Writes go out as
   batched inserts rather than per-row saves. This is where most of the wall-
   clock improvement came from, and it's what makes partial progress durable —
   a failure at row 40,000 doesn't discard the first 39,000.

5. **Retry transient, quarantine permanent.** Transient failures (lock
   contention, connection timeouts, a downstream blip) retry with backoff.
   Permanent failures — genuinely bad data — are quarantined with their reason
   rather than retried forever, and surface in the organiser's error report so
   they can fix and re-submit just those rows.

6. **Make re-runs safe.** Every row carries a deterministic identity derived
   from the file and the business key, and writes are upserts. Re-running a job
   converges to the same state instead of duplicating it. This is the piece that
   makes retries genuinely safe rather than theoretically safe.

7. **Make it observable.** Job status advances as chunks complete, with hot
   progress counters kept in Redis so the UI can poll without hammering the
   primary database. Throughput and error-rate metrics went to Prometheus/Grafana
   through Spring Actuator.

**The parts that were genuinely hard.**

*Partial failure was a product decision, not just a technical one.* I initially
built strict per-file atomicity because it felt "correct." It was wrong for the
users: organisers overwhelmingly preferred 49,800 rows imported plus a precise
report on the 200 that failed, over a clean rejection of all 50,000 hours before
their event. Changing the transaction boundary from per-file to per-chunk, and
treating row-level validation failures as data to report rather than errors to
throw, was the single most important design change. It taught me to go ask what
failure should *mean* to the user before choosing where to put a transaction.

*Throughput isn't monotonic in concurrency.* Raising processing concurrency
improved things up to a point and then made them worse — more workers competed
for a fixed connection pool and increased lock contention, so time went into
waiting rather than working. Tuning concurrency and pool sizing as one coupled
system, instead of separately, was what actually moved the number.

*Isolation from the live platform.* Bounding ingestion concurrency mattered as
much as making it fast. Ingestion is throughput-oriented and can afford to take
longer; the live event path is latency-sensitive and cannot. Deliberately
capping the pipeline so it could never starve live traffic was the right
trade even though it made imports slower in isolation.

*Error messages are a feature.* "Import failed" is worthless. "Row 12,431:
`registration_date` — expected a date, got `N/A`" is something an organiser can
act on without contacting support. Getting validation output to that standard
took real work and removed a support burden.

**Outcome.** The pipeline handled 2,000+ files per batch at 50,000+ rows each,
with resumable jobs, safe retries, per-row error reporting, and no measurable
impact on the live platform during events serving 100K+ concurrent users.

**What I'd do differently.** I'd express schemas as configuration rather than
code, so onboarding a new file format doesn't require a deployment — that
assumption cost me repeatedly. I'd also add per-chunk metrics from day one
instead of retrofitting them; when the first performance problem appeared I was
debugging with far less visibility than I'd have liked.

**The general lesson.** Every meaningful win came from architecture — decoupling
the request from the work, chunking the unit of failure, making re-runs
idempotent — not from micro-optimisation. And the most important question turned
out not to be technical at all: *what should partial success look like to the
person waiting on this data?*

# 2. One thing you're good at technically that not many others are

**The claim to make:** you work on *both sides of the model boundary*. Most
backend engineers treat an ML model as a black box someone else owns; most ML
people can't ship and operate the service around it. You do both — and that seam
is where computer-vision and GenAI products actually fail.

This is your most defensible differentiator because it's unusual *at any level*
and genuinely rare at 1.5 years, and PalletVision is direct evidence.

## The answer

I'm comfortable on both sides of the machine-learning boundary — the model
itself, and the production system around it. Most backend engineers treat a
model as a black box that someone else owns; most ML-focused people can't take
the thing they've built and run it as a reliable service. I do both, and almost
everything useful I've done sits in the seam between them.

At Visionify.ai I own PalletVision end to end as an SDE-1 — the computer-vision
detection, the backend services, and the frontend. It runs in production for
pallet manufacturers, driving productivity tracking, grading and dimensional
analytics. There's no handoff in that product: the same person who changes how
detection behaves also owns what the service does with the output and what the
customer finally sees.

Concretely, here's what that's worth:

**Diagnosing across the boundary.** When output is wrong in production, split
teams stall — the vision side says it's being fed bad frames, the backend side
says the model is wrong, and days disappear into that argument. I can look at
both and tell which it is. That's the single biggest time saving I've seen from
owning both halves.

**Designing the contract between the two.** Model output isn't an API. What the
service does with a low-confidence detection, how uncertainty is represented
downstream, when to drop a frame versus retry it, what "no detection" means to
business logic — those are joint design decisions, and they get made badly when
nobody owns both sides.

**Treating inference as a systems problem.** Latency, throughput, batching, and
what happens when inference is slower than frames arrive are backend problems
that happen to involve a model. I approach them with the same instincts I'd
bring to any high-throughput pipeline — bounded queues, backpressure,
degradation that's deliberate rather than accidental.

**Knowing that evaluation accuracy isn't production accuracy.** A model that
looks strong in evaluation meets real lighting, real camera angles, real
occlusion on a factory floor. Expecting that changes what you build around it —
you design for graceful degradation instead of discovering the gap after
deployment.

The same instinct is why my portfolio runs a real RAG chatbot on a zero-cost
serverless stack rather than a prototype in a notebook: getting an AI feature to
production, cheaply and reliably, is a different skill from getting it to work
once.

To be clear about the limits: I'm not an ML researcher and I won't out-design a
specialist on model architecture. My edge is being a backend engineer who is
genuinely at home inside the model rather than fenced off from it — so nothing
falls through the gap. Most CV and GenAI products fail at productionisation, not
at modelling, and productionisation is exactly the part I'm good at.
